pos: n. (the spy sent from the tribe of Benjamin to search the land of Canaan)
etymology: Hebrew Palti, my deliverance, or the LORD delivers, from palat, to escape or deliver; named once, Numbers 13:9.
biblical_def: Palti is Benjamin's representative among the twelve: “Of the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu” (Numbers 13:9). The commission was explicit: “Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel: of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them” (Numbers 13:2). Note the tense — which I give. The land was already granted; the search was not to determine whether it could be taken but to see what the LORD had given. Ten of the twelve came back and said otherwise: “But the men that went up with him said, We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we” (Numbers 13:31). Palti is not named in the rebellion individually, but he is one of the ten. Only Joshua and Caleb rent their clothes and stood against the congregation. Every one of these men was a ruler of his tribe, chosen for his standing, and ten of them perished by the plague before the LORD. A man whose name means my deliverance died in the wilderness for refusing the deliverance offered.

corruption_summary: The spies' report is read as realistic risk assessment; Scripture calls it an evil report and unbelief, because God had already said the land was given.
corruption_paragraphs: Ten rulers of Israel looked at walled cities and giants and concluded, accurately, that Israel could not take them. The arithmetic was sound and the conclusion was damning, because the question had never been whether Israel was able. The LORD had said, which I give unto the children of Israel. To weigh the obstacles as though the promise were not in the balance is not prudence; the text names it an evil report and the LORD names it unbelief.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faith reckons with what God has said as a fact in the case. Joshua and Caleb saw the same giants and the same walls. “And Joshua the son of Nun, and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, which were of them that searched the land, rent their clothes” (Numbers 14:6) — not because the danger was smaller than reported, but because the LORD was in it.

pos: n. (the father of Palti, the spy of the tribe of Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Raphu, healed, or feared, from rapha, to heal or make whole; named once, Numbers 13:9.
biblical_def: Raphu is known only as a father: “Of the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu” (Numbers 13:9). The chapter names each spy with his patronymic, because each was a ruler among his tribe and the fathers' houses were how authority was identified in Israel. Raphu's name is from the root rapha, to heal — the root behind Jehovah-rapha, the LORD that healeth thee, and behind Rephaim, the name of the giants whose presence in the land so terrified his son's company. What makes the list sober reading is what became of it. Of the twelve men named in Numbers 13 with their fathers' names, two entered Canaan. Moses renamed one of them in that same passage: “And Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua” (Numbers 13:16), the LORD is salvation. Ten fathers' houses are listed in the chapter and ten of those sons died in the wilderness.

corruption_summary: Patronymics are read as archaic formality; in Israel a man's father's house was the public account of who he was and what he answered for.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern identity is self-declared and portable. Israel's was inherited and locatable: a man was named with his father, his father's house and his tribe, and acted under all three. The twelve spies are listed that way because they went as representatives, not as individuals, and their report would bind their tribes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that we are set in families and answer within them, which is the creational order and not a cultural accident. The root of this man's name is the LORD's own self-disclosure at Marah: “I am the LORD that healeth thee” (Exodus 15:26). The fathers of Israel named their sons out of what they knew of God.

pos: n. (the spy sent from the tribe of Asher to search the land of Canaan)
etymology: Hebrew Sethur, hidden, or secreted, from sathar, to hide or conceal; named once, Numbers 13:13.
biblical_def: Sethur is Asher's man among the twelve: “Of the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael” (Numbers 13:13). He went up with the rest, saw what the rest saw, and came back with the ten. The report they brought was not false in its particulars — the land did eat up the inhabitants, the cities were walled and very great, the sons of Anak were there — and it was nonetheless called an evil report, because it was offered as a reason not to obey. His father's name, Michael, asks the question the whole chapter answers: who is like God. The ten answered, in effect, that the Canaanites were. His own name means hidden, and the heart of Israel was uncovered by that fortieth day. What the search revealed was not chiefly the state of Canaan but the state of the congregation, which wept all night and spoke of returning to Egypt.

corruption_paragraphs: The spies' facts were largely correct. That is what makes the episode so searching. “And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel, saying, The land, through which we have gone to search it, is a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof” (Numbers 13:32). The report was evil not because it exaggerated but because it concluded against the word of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that obedience is owed whatever the survey says. The congregation's reaction shows where the argument was always heading: “And wherefore hath the LORD brought us unto this land, to fall by the sword, that our wives and our children should be a prey?” (Numbers 14:3). A man named hidden helped bring the hidden thing out.

pos: n. (the father of Nahbi, the spy of the tribe of Naphtali)
etymology: Hebrew Vophsi, of uncertain derivation, perhaps rich or additional; named once, Numbers 13:14.
biblical_def: Vophsi appears in the shortest possible form: “Of the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vophsi” (Numbers 13:14). Five words establish a tribe, a spy and a father's house. The chapter is a list of twelve such lines, and it is one of the places where Scripture's exactness about names carries the whole moral weight of the story. The men are named individually, before the mission, so that when the judgment falls it falls on named men and not on an anonymous crowd: “Even those men that did bring up the evil report upon the land, died by the plague before the LORD” (Numbers 14:37). Ten out of twelve, each one a ruler of his tribe, each one listed with his father in Numbers 13. Vophsi's name means nothing certain to us; what is certain is that his son is counted among the ten.

corruption_summary: Guilt is diffused into the group so that nobody bears it; Numbers names the ten men, and names the two who did not join them.
corruption_paragraphs: Collective language protects the guilty. Scripture refuses it here with unusual force. The ten are named in chapter 13 before anyone knows what they will say, and the judgment in chapter 14 falls on them by that naming. The two exceptions are named as exceptions: “But Joshua the son of Nun, and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, which were of the men that went to search the land, lived still” (Numbers 14:38).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is personal accountability before God, which is not dissolved by the fact that most of one's colleagues agreed. Ten rulers held the majority and the majority died. Nahbi the son of Vophsi was one of them, and his father's name is in the Bible for it.

pos: n. (the father of Elizaphan, prince of Zebulun at the dividing of the land)
etymology: Hebrew Parnak, of uncertain derivation, possibly of foreign origin; named once, Numbers 34:25.
biblical_def: Parnach belongs to the second list of tribal representatives, taken a generation after the spies: “And the prince of the tribe of the children of Zebulun, Elizaphan the son of Parnach” (Numbers 34:25). The commission this time was not to search the land but to divide it: “These are the names of the men which shall divide the land unto you: Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun” (Numbers 34:17), and “ye shall take one prince of every tribe, to divide the land by inheritance” (Numbers 34:18). The contrast with Numbers 13 is the point of the chapter. The same office — one ruler from each tribe — is filled by a wholly new set of men, because the first set died in the wilderness. Of the names in Numbers 13 only Joshua and Caleb reappear. Parnach's son stands in a dead man's place, dividing a land the previous generation refused to enter.

corruption_summary: A promise delayed is counted a promise broken; the generation that refused Canaan died in the sand and the next generation divided it by lot.
corruption_paragraphs: Forty years is long enough for a people to conclude that God has changed His mind. Numbers 34 answers with a list of surveyors. The boundaries are drawn in detail — the south quarter, the great sea, the east border — and twelve princes are appointed by name to apportion what was promised to Abraham. “These are they whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance unto the children of Israel in the land of Canaan” (Numbers 34:29).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the judgment of one generation does not annul the covenant to the next. The unbelieving died and the promise stood. God buried the men and kept His word, which is the whole argument of Hebrews 3 and 4 and the reason that chapter ends in a warning to us.

pos: n. (prince of the tribe of Naphtali at the dividing of the land)
etymology: Hebrew Pedah'el, God hath redeemed, from padah, to ransom or redeem, with El, God; named once, Numbers 34:28.
biblical_def: Pedahel is the last of the twelve princes named to divide Canaan: “And the prince of the tribe of the children of Naphtali, Pedahel the son of Ammihud” (Numbers 34:28). His name is a sentence of doctrine: God hath redeemed. The root padah is the Exodus word — the LORD redeemed Israel out of the house of bondage, the firstborn were redeemed with a lamb, a life was ransomed by a price paid. A man bearing that confession stands at the moment when the ransomed people take possession of what they were ransomed for. The chapter is a surveyor's document, all borders and apportionments, and it closes, “These are they whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance unto the children of Israel in the land of Canaan” (Numbers 34:29). Redemption in Scripture is never an end in itself; it is deliverance out of something and into something, and Pedahel's commission was the into.

corruption_summary: Redemption is reduced to rescue from a feeling; in Scripture it is a price paid, a people bought, and an inheritance entered.
corruption_paragraphs: The word redeem has been loosened until it means little more than making something good out of something bad. Its biblical sense is commercial and legal: a price is paid and a captive changes hands. “But because the LORD loved you, and because he would keep the oath which he had sworn unto your fathers, hath the LORD brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondmen” (Deuteronomy 7:8).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that redemption terminates in possession. Israel was bought out of Egypt in order to be planted in Canaan, and the princes of Numbers 34 were the men who handed out the deeds. The same shape governs the gospel: a purchase by blood, and “an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away” (1 Peter 1:4).

pos: n. (the father of Kemuel, prince of Ephraim at the dividing of the land)
etymology: Hebrew Shiphtan, judicial, or their judge, from shaphat, to judge or govern; named once, Numbers 34:24.
biblical_def: Shiphtan is named once, as a father: “And the prince of the tribe of the children of Ephraim, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan” (Numbers 34:24). The name comes from shaphat, the root that gives Israel its judges, Jehoshaphat his name, and the Psalms their great refrain that God is judge Himself. It is a fitting name in this chapter, because dividing an inheritance among twelve tribes is a judicial act before it is a surveying one. Disputes over boundaries are the oldest quarrel in settled life, and the LORD did not leave the apportionment to negotiation between the strong and the weak: He named the men, “one prince of every tribe, to divide the land by inheritance” (Numbers 34:18), with Eleazar the priest and Joshua over them, and the allotment was by lot, which is to say by His hand. A man called judicial stands behind the prince of Ephraim in that work.

pos: n. (the man of Gallim to whom Saul gave Michal, David's wife; called Phalti in 1 Samuel)
etymology: Hebrew Paltiel, God is my deliverance, from palat, to deliver, with El, God; named once in this fuller form, 2 Samuel 3:15.
biblical_def: Phaltiel is the second husband of Michal, and his one scene is among the most painful in the books of Samuel. Saul had taken his daughter from David and “had given Michal his daughter, David's wife, to Phalti the son of Laish, which was of Gallim” (1 Samuel 25:44). Years later, with Saul dead and the kingdom turning, David demanded her back as the price of a treaty with Abner, “And Ishbosheth sent, and took her from her husband, even from Phaltiel the son of Laish” (2 Samuel 3:15). Then: “And her husband went with her along weeping behind her to Bahurim. Then said Abner unto him, Go, return. And he returned” (2 Samuel 3:16). Scripture reports the weeping without a word of judgment on it. A marriage that should never have been made was unmade, a man who had loved his wife walked behind her crying until a general told him to go home, and the politics proceeded. The name means God is my deliverance, which in this chapter is a title and not an experience.

corruption_summary: Marriage is treated as an arrangement that power may rearrange; the grief of the man walking behind her is set down in Scripture without excuse for anyone.
corruption_paragraphs: Saul gave away a married woman to punish his son-in-law. David demanded her back to legitimise his claim. Abner delivered her to buy his own position. Three men used one marriage as an instrument of state, and the only person in the chapter who behaves like a husband is the man who is sent home weeping. Scripture records every step and commends none of it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that marriage is a covenant before God, not a political asset, and that the suffering caused by treating it otherwise is real suffering that God sees. “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Matthew 19:6). The Holy Ghost preserved the detail of a man crying as far as Bahurim, which is not the sort of thing a court historian puts in.

pos: n. (the father of the woman Eleazar married, grandfather of Phinehas)
etymology: Hebrew Puti'el, afflicted of God, or God enlightens, of uncertain root with El, God; named once, Exodus 6:25.
biblical_def: Putiel is named once, at the close of the only genealogy in Exodus: “And Eleazar Aaron's son took him one of the daughters of Putiel to wife; and she bare him Phinehas: these are the heads of the fathers of the Levites according to their families” (Exodus 6:25). The placement is deliberate. Moses interrupts the confrontation with Pharaoh to insert the house of Levi, running Levi to Kohath to Amram to Aaron and Moses — “And Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses” (Exodus 6:20) — and then one generation further, to Phinehas. The reason appears centuries of narrative later. Phinehas is the priest who stopped the plague at Baal-peor and received “the covenant of an everlasting priesthood” (Numbers 25:13). Exodus 6 names his mother's father before Israel has left Egypt. The high-priestly line that would run through the whole Old Testament is identified in the middle of the plagues, before there is a priesthood at all.

corruption_summary: A genealogy placed mid-crisis looks like an interruption; Exodus 6 is where God identifies the priestly line before He has delivered the people who will need it.
corruption_paragraphs: The reader wants the plagues to continue and finds nineteen verses of Levite ancestry instead. The placement is the message. Before the first plague falls, the text establishes who Aaron is, who Moses is, and whose grandson Phinehas will be. “These are that Aaron and Moses, to whom the LORD said, Bring out the children of Israel from the land of Egypt according to their armies” (Exodus 6:26).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God provides the ministry before the people know they need it. The priest who would turn away wrath at Peor is named in a list written while Israel was still making bricks. Putiel's only distinction is that his daughter stood in that line.

pos: n. (a prince of Simeon in the days of Hezekiah)
etymology: Hebrew Meshovav, brought back, or restored, from shuv, to turn or return; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:34.
biblical_def: Meshobab heads a short list of Simeonite princes: “And Meshobab, and Jamlech, and Joshah the son of Amaziah” (1 Chronicles 4:34). The passage explains who they were and what they did: “These mentioned by their names were princes in their families: and the house of their fathers increased greatly” (1 Chronicles 4:38); and then, “these written by name came in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and smote their tents, and the habitations that were found there, and destroyed them utterly unto this day, and dwelt in their rooms: because there was pasture there for their flocks” (1 Chronicles 4:41). Simeon had no separate inheritance — Jacob had said he would be scattered in Israel — and so, generations later, its princes went out looking for pasture and took it. The name Meshobab means brought back or restored. He belongs to a tribe under an ancient word of dispersion, and he is named at the one moment in Chronicles where that tribe acts as a tribe and finds land.

corruption_summary: An ancient word of judgment is thought to expire with time; Simeon was still scattered generations later, and still under God's providence within it.
corruption_paragraphs: Jacob's word over Simeon and Levi was severe: “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7). Centuries later Simeon is landless among Judah, its princes hunting pasture in Gedor and on the slopes of Seir. The word held.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's pronouncements govern history long after the men who heard them are dead, and that His providence operates inside the judgment rather than around it. Simeon was scattered and Simeon was fed. A prince named restored led them to the pasture.
